etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English karette and Middle French carotte, both from Latin carōta, from Ancient Greek καρωτόν (karōtón). Doublet of carotte and related to caraway. Displaced native Middle English more, from Old English more, moru (“edible root, parsnip, carrot”), related to German Möhre (“carrot”).

definitions.definition: A vegetable with a nutritious, juicy, sweet root that is often orange in colour, Daucus carota, especially the subspecies sativus in the family Apiaceae.
A shade of orange similar to the flesh of most carrots (also called carrot orange).
(figurative) Any motivational tool; an incentive to do something.

quote.citation: 2022 August 7, Coral Davenport, Lisa Friedman, “Five Decades in the Making: Why It Took Congress So Long to Act on Climate”, in The New York Times‎[1], →ISSN:
quote.text: Essentially, lawmakers replaced the sticks with carrots.

quote.citation: 2023 August 7, Paul Krugman, “Climate Is Now a Culture War Issue”, in The New York Times‎[2]:
quote.text: In 2022, when the Biden administration finally succeeded in passing a major climate bill, it consisted almost entirely of carrots—tax credits and subsidies for green energy.

definitions.definition: (UK, slang, derogatory) Someone from a rural background.
(UK, slang) A police officer from somewhere within the British Isles, but specifically outside of Greater London.
(transitive) To treat (an animal pelt) with a solution of mercuric nitrate as part of felt manufacture.
